\PYG{k}{auto}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{sampled}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{df}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{sample}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+m+mi}{100}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m+mi}{7}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}

\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{head}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{tail}}, and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{view}} are preview\sphinxhyphen{}oriented and return \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{DataFrameView}}.
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{slice}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{take}}, and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{sample}} return \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{DataFrame}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{slice(start, stop)}} uses half\sphinxhyphen{}open row positions: it keeps \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{start}} and stops
before \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{stop}}. Negative slice bounds are normalized against the frame size by
the implementation. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{take(indices)}} uses the exact row positions you provide
and keeps them in that order. Both preserve the selected rows’ original case

\PYG{k}{auto}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{band}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{df}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{query}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{age between 45 and 50}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{k}{auto}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{selected}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{df}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{query}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{job in (\PYGZsq{}management\PYGZsq{}, \PYGZsq{}technician\PYGZsq{})}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{k}{auto}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{combined}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{df}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{query}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{age \PYGZgt{}= 45 and balance \PYGZgt{} 0}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The first table is sorted by \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{price}} descending. The case labels still show
the original row labels, so the first row displays case \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{3}} because Tamale was
the fourth row in the input.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The second table is \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{slice(1, 3)}}. It keeps row positions 1 and 2 and stops
before position 3. The third table is \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{take(\{3, 0\})}}; it keeps exactly Tamale
then Accra because that is the order of the indices.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The fourth table demonstrates feature\sphinxhyphen{}axis work. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{rename("units", "quantity")}}
changes the feature name, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{drop(\{"region"\})}} removes the region feature, and
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{reorder(\{"city", "price", "quantity"\})}} arranges the full remaining feature
set in the requested order.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The fifth table shows \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{label().set("city", true)}}. City values become case labels,
and the original \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{city}} feature is removed because \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{drop\_feature}} is \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{true}}.
The sixth table shows \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{relabel().set("city\_case")}}, which turns the case axis
back into a normal feature named \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{city\_case}} and restores default numeric case
labels.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Use \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{join}} when two frames already have compatible row counts and you want to
append features. Use \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{unify}} when rows must be matched by key values. Use
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{update}} when the right frame should patch values into the left frame. Use
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{combine}} when you need the configurable primitive behind \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{join}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{update}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The names are precise:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{join}} is feature\sphinxhyphen{}wise combination. It requires the same case count and
appends right\sphinxhyphen{}hand features by row position. Duplicate feature names receive
the collision suffix.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{update}} is schema\sphinxhyphen{}preserving patching. It only updates overlapping features
and ignores right\sphinxhyphen{}hand features that do not exist on the left.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{unify}} is key\sphinxhyphen{}based matching. It creates rows for matching key values
and appends right\sphinxhyphen{}hand payload features.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{combine}} is the configurable primitive underneath \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{join}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{update}}.

\end{itemize}

The first result is \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{join}}. The left frame has \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{sku}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{qty}}; the patch frame
has \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{qty}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{status}}. Because \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{qty}} exists on both sides, PlussMic keeps the
left \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{qty}} and appends the right feature as \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{qty\_patch}}. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{status}} is appended
without renaming.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The second result is \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{update}}. Only overlapping features are considered, so
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{qty}} is replaced by the patch values and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{status}} is ignored. This is useful
when the right frame is a correction frame rather than a source of new columns.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The third result is \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{stitch\_on("sku", right, "sku", "\_right")}}. This is the
key\sphinxhyphen{}based operation. Only \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{B}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{C}} appear because those keys exist in both
frames. The right key feature is not duplicated because both key names are
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{sku}}. The right \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{qty}} collides with the left \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{qty}}, so it becomes
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{qty\_right}}; \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{cost}} is appended as a new payload feature.

\subsection{Part VI: Thread Workflows}
\label{\detokenize{manual/part06_thread_workflows:part-vi-thread-workflows}}\label{\detokenize{manual/part06_thread_workflows::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Thread}} is PlussMic’s column model. Every \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{DataFrame}} feature is a named
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Thread}}, and many table operations delegate their real work to Thread methods.
If \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{DataFrame}} is the table abstraction, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Thread}} is the typed one\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional
array abstraction underneath it.

\sphinxAtStartPar
A Thread has four important pieces of state:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
a payload family: \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Series}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Note}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Timeline}}, or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{TimeIndex}};

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
an optional validity mask for missing values;

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
optional display labels;

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
an optional display name.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The payload family controls which operations are legal. Numeric arithmetic is
for \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Series}} threads. Text cleaning is for \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Note}} threads. Calendar extraction
is for \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Timeline}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{TimeIndex}} threads. Missingness is tracked separately
through the validity mask, so a row can have a stored payload value and still
display as \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{NA}}.


\subsubsection{Payload families}
\label{\detokenize{manual/part06_thread_workflows:payload-families}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
The public kind enum is:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{enum}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{class}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nc}{ThreadKind}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{Series}\PYG{p}{,}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{Note}\PYG{p}{,}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{Timeline}\PYG{p}{,}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{TimeIndex}\PYG{p}{,}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Use the family\sphinxhyphen{}specific accessors only after you know the kind:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{if}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{k+kr}{thread}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{kind}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pluss}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{table}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{ThreadKind}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{Series}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{k}{const}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{auto}\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{values}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kr}{thread}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{as\PYGZus{}series}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}

\PYG{k}{if}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{k+kr}{thread}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{kind}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pluss}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{table}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{ThreadKind}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{Note}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{k}{const}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{auto}\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{text}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kr}{thread}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{as\PYGZus{}note}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Calling the wrong accessor is an error. For example, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{as\_series()}} is only valid
for a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Series}} payload.


\subsubsection{Construct threads}
\label{\detokenize{manual/part06_thread_workflows:construct-threads}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Numeric values normally enter a Thread through \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{pluss::make\_series}}:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{pluss}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{table}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{Thread}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{numeric}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pluss}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{make\PYGZus{}series}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}\PYG{l+m+mf}{1.0}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m+mf}{2.0}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m+mf}{3.0}\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Text values normally enter through \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{pluss::make\_note}}:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{pluss}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{table}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{Thread}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{text}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pluss}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{make\PYGZus{}note}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{alpha}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{beta}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{gamma}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
You can attach a validity mask at construction time:

\subsubsection{Inspect a Thread}
\label{\detokenize{manual/part06_thread_workflows:inspect-a-thread}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Use these methods when writing generic code:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]

\PYG{k+kr}{thread}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{kind}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{k+kr}{thread}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{dtype}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{k+kr}{thread}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{is\PYGZus{}valid}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+m+mi}{0}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{k+kr}{thread}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{isnull}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{k+kr}{thread}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{notnull}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{dtype()}} reports the payload dtype, such as \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{float64}} or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{utf8}}. It does
not tell you whether the thread has missing values. Use \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{isnull()}},
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{notnull()}}, or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{is\_valid(row)}} for that.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{to\_string()}} is useful in tests, examples, and documentation because it uses
the same display path a user sees.

\subsubsection{Row\sphinxhyphen{}space operations}
\label{\detokenize{manual/part06_thread_workflows:row-space-operations}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A Thread is one\sphinxhyphen{}dimensional, so row\sphinxhyphen{}space operations work directly on element
positions:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kr}{thread}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{head}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+m+mi}{5}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{k+kr}{thread}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{tail}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+m+mi}{5}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{k+kr}{thread}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{view}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+m+mi}{10}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m+mi}{20}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{k+kr}{thread}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{slice}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+m+mi}{10}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m+mi}{20}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{k+kr}{thread}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{take}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{std}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{vector}\PYG{o}{\PYGZlt{}}\PYG{n}{std}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{k+kt}{int64\PYGZus{}t}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}\PYG{l+m+mi}{0}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m+mi}{3}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m+mi}{8}\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{k+kr}{thread}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{shift}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{k+kr}{thread}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{sort\PYGZus{}values}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n+nb}{true}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nb}{true}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{k+kr}{thread}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{dropnull}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{k+kr}{thread}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{distinct}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n+nb}{true}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{head}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{tail}}, and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{view}} return \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ThreadView}}, which can auto\sphinxhyphen{}render. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{slice}},
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{take}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{shift}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{sort\_values}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{dropnull}}, and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{distinct}} return ordinary
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Thread}} values.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{slice(start, stop)}} is half\sphinxhyphen{}open. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{take(indices)}} keeps exactly the requested
positions in exactly that order. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{shift(periods)}} moves values by row offset
and marks the newly exposed edge as missing. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{sort\_values(ascending, nulls\_last)}} sorts the valid values and places masked rows according to
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{nulls\_last}}.


\subsubsection{Missingness}
\label{\detokenize{manual/part06_thread_workflows:missingness}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Missingness is mask\sphinxhyphen{}based. A Thread without a validity mask has no mask\sphinxhyphen{}level
missing values. A Thread with a validity mask uses \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{true}} for present and
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{false}} for missing.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Common methods:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{auto}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{missing}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kr}{thread}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{isnull}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{k}{auto}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{present}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kr}{thread}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{notnull}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{k}{auto}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{complete}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kr}{thread}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{dropnull}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{k}{auto}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{forward}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kr}{thread}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{ffill}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{k}{auto}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{backward}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kr}{thread}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{bfill}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Numeric checks are separate:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{auto}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{nan}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kr}{thread}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{isnan}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{k}{auto}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{finite}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kr}{thread}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{isfinite}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{isnan()}} checks floating\sphinxhyphen{}point NaN in a Series payload. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{isnull()}} checks the
Thread validity mask. A value can be finite but masked out, and it will still
display as \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{NA}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{score}} payload has five numeric values, but row 2 is masked as missing,
so it displays as \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{NA}}. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{isnull()}} is the logical inverse of the validity mask.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{fillnull(99.0)}} keeps the valid values \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{4}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{1}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{3}}, and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{2}}, and replaces only
the masked row with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{99}}. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{dropnull()}} removes the masked row. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{shift(2)}} moves
values down by two rows, marks rows 0 and 1 missing because there are no source
values for them, and also carries the original missing row forward so row 4 is
missing. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{sort\_values}} with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{nulls\_last=false}} places the missing value first,
then sorts valid values ascending. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{take(\{4, 1, 0\})}} keeps rows 4, 1, and 0, in
that order.


\subsubsection{Numeric operations}
\label{\detokenize{manual/part06_thread_workflows:numeric-operations}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Series\sphinxhyphen{}backed Threads support arithmetic, comparisons, math transforms, rolling
windows, and scalar reductions.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Arithmetic can be written through methods or operators:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{auto}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{plus\PYGZus{}two}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kr}{thread}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{+}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m+mf}{2.0}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{k}{auto}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{doubled}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kr}{thread}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m+mf}{2.0}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{k}{auto}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{ratio}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{numerator}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{/}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{denominator}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{k}{auto}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{remainder}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kr}{thread}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZpc{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m+mf}{2.0}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Comparison operators return boolean Series\sphinxhyphen{}backed Threads:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{auto}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{positive}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kr}{thread}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m+mf}{0.0}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{k}{auto}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{in\PYGZus{}limit}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kr}{thread}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZlt{}}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m+mf}{100.0}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{k}{auto}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{same}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{left}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{right}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Named numeric transforms:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{auto}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{absolute}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kr}{thread}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{abs}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{k}{auto}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{clipped}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kr}{thread}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{clip}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+m+mf}{0.0}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m+mf}{100.0}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{k}{auto}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{logged}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kr}{thread}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{log}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{k}{auto}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{exponentiated}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kr}{thread}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{exp}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{k+kt}{double}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{mean}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kr}{thread}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{mean}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{item}\PYG{o}{\PYGZlt{}}\PYG{k+kt}{double}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{auto}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{gt\PYGZus{}zero}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kr}{thread}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{compare}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+m+mf}{0.0}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pluss}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{table}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{ThreadBinaryCompareOp}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{Gt}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{k}{auto}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{le\PYGZus{}other}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kr}{thread}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{compare}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{other}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pluss}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{table}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{ThreadBinaryCompareOp}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{Le}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]

\PYG{k}{auto}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{half\PYGZus{}open}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kr}{thread}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{btw}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+m+mf}{10.0}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m+mf}{20.0}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nb}{true}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nb}{false}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{k}{auto}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{text\PYGZus{}band}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{text}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{btw}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{a}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{m}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nb}{true}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}

\subsubsection{Rolling windows}
\label{\detokenize{manual/part06_thread_workflows:rolling-windows}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Use \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{window}} for simple rolling aggregations over numeric Series payloads:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{auto}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{rolling\PYGZus{}sum}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kr}{thread}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{window}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+m+mi}{3}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pluss}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{table}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{ThreadWindowOp}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{RollingSum}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{k}{auto}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{rolling\PYGZus{}mean}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kr}{thread}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{window}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+m+mi}{3}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pluss}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{table}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{ThreadWindowOp}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{RollingMean}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m+mi}{2}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{k}{auto}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{rolling\PYGZus{}min}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kr}{thread}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{window}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+m+mi}{5}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pluss}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{table}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{ThreadWindowOp}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{RollingMin}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m+mi}{3}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{k}{auto}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{rolling\PYGZus{}max}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kr}{thread}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{window}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+m+mi}{5}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pluss}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{table}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{ThreadWindowOp}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{RollingMax}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m+mi}{3}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The arguments are:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{window}}: number of rows in the trailing window;

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{op}}: rolling operation;

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{min\_periods}}: minimum number of valid observations required for an output
value.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
If a row does not have enough valid observations, the output row is masked and
prints as \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{NA}}.


\subsubsection{Thread time\sphinxhyphen{}series accessor}
\label{\detokenize{manual/part06_thread_workflows:thread-time-series-accessor}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{thread.ts()}} is for one numeric value stream. It does not need a separate
date feature for operations such as returns, lag, lead, rolling mean, or
expanding statistics.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Casting rules are family\sphinxhyphen{}specific:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Series to Series changes numeric dtype.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Series to Note formats each scalar as text.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Series to Timeline treats numeric values as either epoch nanoseconds or
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{YYYYMMDD}} values when all valid rows look like dates.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Note to Series parses bools or numbers depending on the requested dtype.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Note to Timeline parses date/time text.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Timeline and TimeIndex can be converted to Note or numeric epoch\sphinxhyphen{}nanosecond
Series.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Parsing failures become invalid rows where supported by the implementation.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{values + 3}} performs elementwise numeric addition. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{btw(2.0, 8.0, true)}} marks
the values \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{2}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{4}}, and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{8}} as true because the interval is inclusive.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The rolling mean uses a trailing window of three rows and requires at least two
observations. Row 0 has only one observation, so it prints \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{NA}}. Row 1 averages
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{1}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{2}}, giving \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{1.5}}. Row 4 averages \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{4}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{8}}, and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{16}}, giving
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{9.333333333}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{returns(1)}} computes one\sphinxhyphen{}period fractional returns. The first row has no
previous value and prints \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{nan}}; every later value doubles from the previous
row, so each return is \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{1}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Casting \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{labels}} to a Float64 Series parses \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{"10"}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{"20"}}, and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{"40"}}. The
string \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{"bad"}} cannot be parsed as a number, so that row is invalid and prints
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{NA}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The text example first replaces hyphens with spaces and then lowercases. The
contains check is performed on the lowercased values, so it matches both
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{North\sphinxhyphen{}East}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{north\sphinxhyphen{}west}}.

\PYG{k}{auto}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{months}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{dates}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{month}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{k}{auto}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{days}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{dates}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{day}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{k}{auto}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{hours}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{dates}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{hour}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{k}{auto}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{weekdays}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{dates}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{to\PYGZus{}note\PYGZus{}weekday}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
These return Threads so they can be inserted back into a DataFrame:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{auto}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{enriched}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{df}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{set}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{year}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{df}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{features}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{timestamp}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{year}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
If you need to parse string dates, cast a Note\sphinxhyphen{}backed Thread to Timeline first:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{auto}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{timeline}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{text\PYGZus{}dates}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{cast}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{pluss}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{table}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{ThreadCastTarget}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{Timeline}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{k}{auto}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{months}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{timeline}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{month}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsubsection{Display labels and names}
\label{\detokenize{manual/part06_thread_workflows:display-labels-and-names}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Display metadata is useful for presentation, but it should not be treated as
schema truth.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{auto}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{named}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kr}{thread}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{with\PYGZus{}display\PYGZus{}name}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{balance}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{k}{auto}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{labeled}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{named}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{with\PYGZus{}display\PYGZus{}labels}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{labels}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{n}{named}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{show}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{n}{std}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{cout}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZlt{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZlt{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{named}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{to\PYGZus{}string}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZlt{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZlt{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s+sc}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s+sc}{\PYGZbs{}n}\PYG{l+s+sc}{\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
For DataFrames, feature names are the schema. Thread display names are just
presentation metadata.


\subsubsection{Functional and mutating methods}
\label{\detokenize{manual/part06_thread_workflows:functional-and-mutating-methods}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Thread transforms are functional by default:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{auto}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{filled}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kr}{thread}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{fillnull}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+m+mf}{0.0}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{k}{auto}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{clipped}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kr}{thread}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{clip}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+m+mf}{0.0}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m+mf}{1.0}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{k}{auto}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{shifted}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k+kr}{thread}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{shift}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The original Thread is unchanged unless you use a mutating method with a
trailing underscore:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k+kr}{thread}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{fillnull\PYGZus{}}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+m+mf}{0.0}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Use mutating methods when mutation is intentional and local. Use functional
methods when building pipelines or returning values from helper functions.


\subsubsection{Choosing Thread or DataFrame APIs}
\label{\detokenize{manual/part06_thread_workflows:choosing-thread-or-dataframe-apis}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Use Thread directly when:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
you are transforming one feature;

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
you need a reusable mask;

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
you are writing a DataFrame \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{assign}} lambda;

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
you need payload\sphinxhyphen{}specific methods such as \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{lower}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{contains}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{year}}, or
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{window}};

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
you want scalar reductions such as \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{mean().item\textless{}double\textgreater{}()}}.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Use DataFrame methods when:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
the operation uses multiple features;

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
you need to preserve feature names;

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
you need table\sphinxhyphen{}shaped output;

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
you are loading, saving, joining, grouping, or pivoting.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The common pattern is to use DataFrame for structure and Thread for feature
logic:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{auto}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{enriched}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{df}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{assign}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{clean\PYGZus{}city}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{k}{const}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pluss}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{table}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{DataFrame}\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{frame}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
\PYG{+w}{      }\PYG{k}{return}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{frame}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{features}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{city}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{replace}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZhy{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{lower}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{p}{,}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxstepscope


\subsection{Part VII: Query Expressions and SQL}
\label{\detokenize{manual/part07_query_sql:part-vii-query-expressions-and-sql}}\label{\detokenize{manual/part07_query_sql::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
PlussMic gives you three practical ways to choose rows:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{DataFrame::query(...)}} evaluates a text predicate against the current frame.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{DataFrame::filter(...)}} applies an explicit boolean mask that you build in C++.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{DataFrame::sql(...).execute(...)}} parses a small SQL \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{SELECT}} language for projection, joins, parameters, ordering, and limits.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The important design point is that these are not three unrelated systems. The SQL executor parses the SQL statement, builds an intermediate \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{DataFrame}}, and sends the SQL \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{WHERE}} clause to \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{DataFrame::query}}. That means SQL \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{WHERE}} supports the same predicate language as \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{query}}, while SQL itself is responsible for \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{SELECT}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{FROM}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{JOIN}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ORDER BY}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LIMIT}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{OFFSET}}, and parameter replacement.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Use \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{query}} when you only need row filtering. Use SQL when you also want column projection, source binding, a join, a limit, or late\sphinxhyphen{}bound parameters. Use an explicit mask when your predicate is easier or safer to express as ordinary C++ code.


\subsubsection{Query expressions}
\label{\detokenize{manual/part07_query_sql:query-expressions}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{DataFrame::query}} takes a predicate string and returns a new frame containing only the cases for which that predicate is true. The result keeps the same feature set as the input frame unless you later select or drop features.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{auto}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{older}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{df}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{query}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{age \PYGZgt{}= 45}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{k}{auto}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{positive}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{df}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{query}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{balance \PYGZgt{} 0}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{k}{auto}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{known}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{df}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{query}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{job != \PYGZsq{}unknown\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{k}{auto}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{band}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{df}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{query}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{age between 45 and 50}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{k}{auto}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{selected}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{df}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{query}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{job in (\PYGZsq{}management\PYGZsq{}, \PYGZsq{}technician\PYGZsq{})}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{k}{auto}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{combined}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{df}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{query}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{age \PYGZgt{}= 45 and balance \PYGZgt{} 0}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
A query string names features directly. Numeric comparisons use numeric features. String comparisons use quoted string literals. Boolean combinations use words such as \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{and}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{or}}.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Use query expressions for:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
filtering a frame without changing its columns;

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
readable conditions in analysis code;

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
direct comparisons against literals;

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
membership checks;

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
range checks;

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
null filtering through helper predicates.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Examples:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{auto}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{clean\PYGZus{}balance}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{df}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{query}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{isnotnull(balance)}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{k}{auto}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{clean\PYGZus{}job}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{df}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{query}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{isnotnull(job) and job != \PYGZsq{}\PYGZsq{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{k}{auto}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{adults\PYGZus{}with\PYGZus{}income}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{df}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{query}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{age \PYGZgt{}= 18 and income \PYGZgt{} 0}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Because \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{query}} works from feature names, treat those names as part of your data contract. If a CSV column is renamed from \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{balance}} to \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{account\_balance}}, every query using \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{balance}} must change.


\subsubsection{Query result shape}
\label{\detokenize{manual/part07_query_sql:query-result-shape}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A query filters cases, not features. If the input frame has 20 features and the predicate matches 5 cases, the output has 5 cases and the same 20 features.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This is why a common workflow is:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{auto}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{filtered}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{df}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{query}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{age \PYGZgt{}= 45 and balance \PYGZgt{} 0}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{k}{auto}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{compact}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{filtered}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{features}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{age}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{job}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{balance}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The first line chooses rows. The second line chooses columns.


\subsubsection{Explicit masks}
\label{\detokenize{manual/part07_query_sql:explicit-masks}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Use a boolean mask when the condition is easier to express in C++ than in the text predicate language. A mask must have one boolean value for each case in the frame. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{true}} keeps the row. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{false}} removes it.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{auto}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{values}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{df}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{features}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{age}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{as\PYGZus{}series}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{to\PYGZus{}vec}\PYG{o}{\PYGZlt{}}\PYG{n}{std}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{k+kt}{int64\PYGZus{}t}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{k}{auto}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{mask}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pluss}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{Series}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{zeros}\PYG{p}{(}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}\PYG{k}{static\PYGZus{}cast}\PYG{o}{\PYGZlt{}}\PYG{n}{std}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{k+kt}{int64\PYGZus{}t}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{values}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{size}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{p}{,}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{n}{pluss}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{codem}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{ScalarType}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{Bool}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{k}{auto}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{keep}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{reinterpret\PYGZus{}cast}\PYG{o}{\PYGZlt{}}\PYG{k+kt}{bool}\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{mask}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{raw\PYGZus{}data}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{k}{for}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{std}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{k+kt}{size\PYGZus{}t}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{i}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m+mi}{0}\PYG{p}{;}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{i}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZlt{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{values}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{size}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{+}\PYG{o}{+}\PYG{n}{i}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
\PYG{+w}{  }\PYG{n}{keep}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{i}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{values}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{i}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZgt{}}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m+mi}{45}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{values}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{n}{i}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZlt{}}\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m+mi}{50}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}

\PYG{k}{auto}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{filtered}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{df}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{filter}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{mask}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This style is more verbose than \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{df.query("age between 45 and 50")}}, but it gives you full control. It is useful when the predicate calls your own C++ functions, depends on external state, or must be debugged step by step.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Use masks when:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
the predicate is a C++ function;

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
the predicate depends on a lookup table or an object that is not a feature;

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
you already computed a boolean \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Series}};

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
you want to inspect the mask before filtering;

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
you need precise control over exceptional cases.

\end{itemize}


\subsubsection{SQL is a PlussMic SELECT language}
\label{\detokenize{manual/part07_query_sql:sql-is-a-plussmic-select-language}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{DataFrame::sql()}} returns a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{DataFrameSqlAccessor}}. The accessor executes \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{SELECT}} statements over the calling frame and optional bound sources.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{auto}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{result}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{df}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{sql}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{execute}\PYG{p}{(}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{SELECT age, job, balance FROM df WHERE age \PYGZgt{}= 45}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The current SQL implementation supports \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{SELECT}} statements only. Non\sphinxhyphen{}\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{SELECT}} statements such as \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{DELETE FROM df}} are rejected. This SQL layer is for shaping in\sphinxhyphen{}memory frames, not mutating databases.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The calling frame is named \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{df}} by default:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{SELECT}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{age}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{job}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{FROM}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{df}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
You may alias the calling frame:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{SELECT}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{customers}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{age}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{FROM}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{df}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{AS}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{customers}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The parser supports:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{SELECT *}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{SELECT feature}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{SELECT feature AS alias}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
qualified names such as \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{df.age}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{FROM df}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{FROM df AS alias}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{JOIN name ON left\_feature = right\_feature}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{WHERE ...}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ORDER BY feature ASC}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ORDER BY feature DESC}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ORDER BY feature ASC NULLS FIRST}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ORDER BY feature ASC NULLS LAST}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LIMIT n}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{OFFSET n}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
scalar parameters such as \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\{min\_age\}}}

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
identifier parameters such as \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\{@feature\_name\}}}

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
There are deliberate limits. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ORDER BY}} accepts one feature key. Projection items are feature names or aliases, not arbitrary expressions. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{WHERE}} expressions are handled by \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{DataFrame::query}}, so use the query predicate language there rather than expecting a full external SQL dialect.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{sales\_frame()}} helper builds this input:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
city    region  units  price
Accra   south   10     3
Tema    south   7      4
Kumasi  middle  12     2.5
Tamale  north   5      5
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The example first derives \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{revenue = units * price}}, then runs three SQL variants over the enriched frame.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Verified output:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
=== 09 sql ===
======================
     | city    revenue
\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}
0    | Accra   30     
2    | Kumasi  30     
\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}
[2 cs x 2 feat]
======================
     | city    revenue
\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}
0    | Accra   30     
2    | Kumasi  30     
1    | Tema    28     
\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}
[3 cs x 2 feat]
=============
     | city  
\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}
0    | Accra 
2    | Kumasi
\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}\PYGZhy{}
[2 cs x 1 feat]
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The first result has two features, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{city}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{revenue}}, because the SQL projection is \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{SELECT city, revenue}}. The \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{WHERE revenue \textgreater{}= 28}} predicate keeps Accra, Kumasi, and Tema, then \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ORDER BY revenue DESC LIMIT 2}} returns only the first two after sorting. Accra and Kumasi both have revenue \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{30}}, so both appear before Tema.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The second result uses two different parameter systems. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\{min\_revenue\}}} is a scalar parameter and becomes the numeric value \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{28}}. \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{\{@value\_col\}}} is an identifier parameter and becomes the feature name \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{revenue}}. Identifier parameters are for column names, not values. They are rendered as escaped SQL identifiers by PlussMic before parsing.

\sphinxAtStartPar
The third result uses a prepared SQL statement. The statement template is created once with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{prepare\_sql}}, and the values are supplied when \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{execute}} is called. The projection only asks for \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{city}}, so the output has one feature.


\subsubsection{SQL options}
\label{\detokenize{manual/part07_query_sql:sql-options}}

\PYG{n}{options}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{identifier\PYGZus{}params}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{value\PYGZus{}col}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{balance}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{n}{options}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{max\PYGZus{}result\PYGZus{}rows}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m+mi}{1000}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{n}{options}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{timeout\PYGZus{}ms}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m+mi}{5000}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{n}{options}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{diagnostics\PYGZus{}explain}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nb}{true}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{k}{auto}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{result}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{df}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{sql}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{options}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{execute}\PYG{p}{(}

\subsubsection{Scalar parameters}
\label{\detokenize{manual/part07_query_sql:scalar-parameters}}

Scalar parameters are placeholders wrapped in braces:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{DataFrame}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{SqlOptions}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{options}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{n}{options}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{params}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{min\PYGZus{}age}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{std}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{k+kt}{int64\PYGZus{}t}\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}\PYG{l+m+mi}{45}\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{n}{options}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{params}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{blocked\PYGZus{}job}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{std}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{string}\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{unknown}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{n}{options}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{params}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{limit\PYGZus{}n}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{std}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{k+kt}{int64\PYGZus{}t}\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}\PYG{l+m+mi}{4}\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{k}{auto}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{out}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{df}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{sql}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{std}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{move}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{options}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{execute}\PYG{p}{(}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{SELECT age, job FROM df }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{WHERE age \PYGZgt{}= \PYGZob{}min\PYGZus{}age\PYGZcb{} and job != \PYGZob{}blocked\PYGZus{}job\PYGZcb{} }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{ORDER BY age DESC LIMIT \PYGZob{}limit\PYGZus{}n\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The SQL renderer turns numbers into SQL numeric tokens, strings into quoted SQL string literals, bools into \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{true}} or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{false}}, and null values into \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{null}}. This happens before parsing, so the parser receives a normal SQL\sphinxhyphen{}like statement after parameter substitution.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Use scalar parameters for values only. Do not use them for column names. For column names, use identifier parameters.


\subsubsection{Identifier parameters}
\label{\detokenize{manual/part07_query_sql:identifier-parameters}}

Identifier parameters are placeholders with \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{@}} after the opening brace:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]

\PYG{n}{options}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{params}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{limit\PYGZus{}n}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{std}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{k+kt}{int64\PYGZus{}t}\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}\PYG{l+m+mi}{2}\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{k}{auto}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{out}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{df}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{sql}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{std}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{move}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{options}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{execute}\PYG{p}{(}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{SELECT \PYGZob{}@col\PYGZcb{} FROM df LIMIT \PYGZob{}limit\PYGZus{}n\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This is safer and clearer than concatenating a feature name into the SQL string yourself. PlussMic validates identifier parameter values before rendering them.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Use identifier parameters for:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
selected feature names;

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
order\sphinxhyphen{}by feature names;

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
source names when they are part of a supported identifier position;

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
aliases where supported by the parser.

\end{itemize}

\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{k}{auto}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{second}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{prepared}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{execute}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{min\PYGZus{}age}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{std}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{k+kt}{int64\PYGZus{}t}\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}\PYG{l+m+mi}{55}\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{p}{,}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{limit\PYGZus{}n}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{std}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{k+kt}{int64\PYGZus{}t}\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}\PYG{l+m+mi}{10}\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{p}{,}

\PYG{+w}{        }\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{limit\PYGZus{}n}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{std}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{k+kt}{int64\PYGZus{}t}\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}\PYG{l+m+mi}{5}\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{p}{,}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{p}{,}

\label{\detokenize{manual/part07_query_sql:case-axis-projection}}

The case axis is not a normal feature unless you ask SQL to expose it. Configure \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{case\_axis\_aliases}} when you want case labels in the result:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{auto}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{with\PYGZus{}case}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{df}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{sql}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{DataFrame}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{SqlOptions}\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{case\PYGZus{}axis\PYGZus{}aliases}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{case}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{idx}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{p}{,}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{execute}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{SELECT idx, age FROM df ORDER BY age DESC LIMIT 3}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
In this example, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{idx}} becomes a projected output feature representing the original case labels. Without \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{case\_axis\_aliases}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{SELECT idx}} would be treated like a normal feature lookup and would fail unless the frame actually had a feature named \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{idx}}.

\label{\detokenize{manual/part07_query_sql:joins}}

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{DataFrame}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{metrics}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}

\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{score}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{df}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{features}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{balance}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{p}{,}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{k}{auto}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{joined}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{df}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{sql}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{DataFrame}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{SqlOptions}\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{sources}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{m}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{n}{metrics}\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{p}{,}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{execute}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{SELECT df.age, m.score FROM df JOIN m ON df.age = m.age LIMIT 6}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

The join source is named \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{m}}, so the SQL statement can refer to \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{m.age}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{m.score}}. Joined right\sphinxhyphen{}hand columns are prefixed internally with the joined source alias, which is why qualified projections such as \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{m.score}} are useful.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Keep joins narrow. Set \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{max\_intermediate\_rows}} when joining data that could expand unexpectedly.

\label{\detokenize{manual/part07_query_sql:collision-policy}}

SQL projection names must be unique by default:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{SELECT}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{age}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{as}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{v}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{balance}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{as}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{v}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{FROM}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{df}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{LIMIT}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m+mi}{3}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This projection asks for two output features with the same name, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{v}}, so the default collision policy rejects it.

\sphinxAtStartPar
Use suffixing if you want PlussMic to keep both:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]

\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{collision\PYGZus{}policy}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{DataFrame}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{SqlOptions}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{CollisionPolicy}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{Suffix}\PYG{p}{,}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{execute}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{SELECT age as v, balance as v FROM df LIMIT 3}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The result has \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{v}} and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{v\_2}}.

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]

\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{collision\PYGZus{}policy}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{DataFrame}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{SqlOptions}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{CollisionPolicy}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{Overwrite}\PYG{p}{,}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{execute}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{SELECT age as v, balance as v FROM df LIMIT 3}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The result keeps one \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{v}}.


\subsubsection{Choosing the right tool}
\label{\detokenize{manual/part07_query_sql:choosing-the-right-tool}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Use \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{query}} when:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
you only need to filter rows;

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
you want the output to keep all features;

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
the predicate is short and readable;

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
you do not need joins or SQL parameters.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Use SQL when:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
you want projection and filtering in one expression;

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
you need \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ORDER BY}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{LIMIT}}, or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{OFFSET}};

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
you need to bind scalar or identifier parameters;

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
you need to join against additional named frames;

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
you want execution guards such as \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{max\_result\_rows}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{max\_intermediate\_rows}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{memory\_budget\_mb}}, or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{timeout\_ms}}.

\end{itemize}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Use explicit masks when:
\begin{itemize}
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
the predicate is ordinary C++ logic;

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
you need custom functions;

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
you need external state;

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
you already have a boolean \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Series}};

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
you want to debug every intermediate value.

\end{itemize}


\subsubsection{Common mistakes}
\label{\detokenize{manual/part07_query_sql:common-mistakes}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Do not use SQL for mutation:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{df}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{sql}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{execute}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{DELETE FROM df}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{c+c1}{// rejected}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Do not use scalar parameters for feature names:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{c+c1}{// Wrong: renders the string as a SQL string literal, not an identifier.}
\PYG{n}{options}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{params}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{col}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{std}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{string}\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{age}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{n}{df}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{sql}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{options}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{execute}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{SELECT \PYGZob{}col\PYGZcb{} FROM df}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Use an identifier parameter instead:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{options}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{identifier\PYGZus{}params}\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{col}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{age}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{n}{df}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{sql}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{n}{options}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{execute}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{SELECT \PYGZob{}@col\PYGZcb{} FROM df}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Do not expect projection expressions:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{SELECT}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{units}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{price}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{AS}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{revenue}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{k}{FROM}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{df}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Derive the feature first, then select it:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{auto}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{enriched}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{df}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{assign}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{revenue}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{p}{[}\PYG{p}{]}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{k}{const}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{DataFrame}\PYG{o}{\PYGZam{}}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{frame}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
\PYG{+w}{      }\PYG{k}{return}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{frame}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{features}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{units}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{*}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{frame}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{features}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{price}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{p}{,}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{k}{auto}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{result}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{enriched}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{sql}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{execute}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{SELECT revenue FROM df}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Do not assume SQL \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{WHERE}} is an external database dialect. It is PlussMic’s DataFrame query predicate language inside a SQL statement.

\sphinxstepscope


\subsection{Part VIII: Time\sphinxhyphen{}Series Workflows}
\label{\detokenize{manual/part08_time_series:part-viii-time-series-workflows}}\label{\detokenize{manual/part08_time_series::doc}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Time\sphinxhyphen{}series work in PlussMic is built from two ideas:
\begin{enumerate}
\sphinxsetlistlabels{\arabic}{enumi}{enumii}{}{.}%
\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
A time axis is data, usually a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Timeline}} or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{TimeIndex}} stored in a
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Thread}}.

\item {} 
\sphinxAtStartPar
Time\sphinxhyphen{}series calculations are ordinary table transformations that return
either a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Thread}} or a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{DataFrame}}.

\end{enumerate}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Use the Thread accessor when you are working on one numeric value stream:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{auto}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{returns}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{df}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{features}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{close}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{ts}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{returns}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Use the DataFrame accessor when you want to transform one or more named
features and keep a table\sphinxhyphen{}shaped result:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{auto}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{returns}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{df}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{features}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{close}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{volume}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{ts}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{returns}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Use DataFrame resampling and reindexing when the operation needs a time axis:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{auto}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{values}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{df}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{label}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{set}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{date}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nb}{false}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{features}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{close}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{volume}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{k}{auto}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{daily}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{values}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{ts}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{resample}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{D}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{mean}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The accessors do not guess that a feature named \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{"date"}} is time\sphinxhyphen{}like. For
cases\sphinxhyphen{}based resampling, the frame cases must actually be a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Timeline}} or
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{TimeIndex}}; use \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{.tl()}} for datetime columns and \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{.ts()}} for numeric value
streams.

\sphinxAtStartPar
If a date column starts as text, parse it through explicit \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{cast(...)}} first:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{auto}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{parsed}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{df}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{cast}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{n}{pluss}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{table}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{DataFrame}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{CastSpec}\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
\PYG{+w}{        }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{date\PYGZus{}text}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,}
\PYG{+w}{        }\PYG{n}{pluss}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{table}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{ThreadCastTarget}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{Timeline}\PYG{p}{,}
\PYG{+w}{        }\PYG{n}{pluss}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{table}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{ThreadCastOptions}\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
\PYG{+w}{            }\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{format}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZpc{}Y\PYGZhy{}\PYGZpc{}m\PYGZhy{}\PYGZpc{}d}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,}
\PYG{+w}{            }\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{invalid}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pluss}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{table}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{ParseInvalid}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{Null}\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{p}{,}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}


\subsubsection{The time data model}
\label{\detokenize{manual/part08_time_series:the-time-data-model}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
PlussMic represents time in three common ways:


\begin{savenotes}\sphinxattablestart
\sphinxthistablewithglobalstyle
\centering
\begin{tabulary}{\linewidth}[t]{TT}
\sphinxtoprule
\begin{varwidth}[t]{\sphinxcolwidth{1}{2}}
\sphinxstyletheadfamily \sphinxAtStartPar
Representation
\sphinxbeforeendvarwidth
\end{varwidth}%
&\begin{varwidth}[t]{\sphinxcolwidth{1}{2}}
\sphinxstyletheadfamily \sphinxAtStartPar
Meaning
\sphinxbeforeendvarwidth
\end{varwidth}%
\\
\sphinxmidrule
\sphinxtableatstartofbodyhook\begin{varwidth}[t]{\sphinxcolwidth{1}{2}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Timeline}}
\sphinxbeforeendvarwidth
\end{varwidth}%
&\begin{varwidth}[t]{\sphinxcolwidth{1}{2}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A sequence of timestamps. Use it for date/time columns.
\sphinxbeforeendvarwidth
\end{varwidth}%
\\
\sphinxhline\begin{varwidth}[t]{\sphinxcolwidth{1}{2}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{TimeIndex}}
\sphinxbeforeendvarwidth
\end{varwidth}%
&\begin{varwidth}[t]{\sphinxcolwidth{1}{2}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A timeline with index semantics. Use it when alignment and as\sphinxhyphen{}of operations matter.
\sphinxbeforeendvarwidth
\end{varwidth}%
\\
\sphinxhline\begin{varwidth}[t]{\sphinxcolwidth{1}{2}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Numeric \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Series}}
\sphinxbeforeendvarwidth
\end{varwidth}%
&\begin{varwidth}[t]{\sphinxcolwidth{1}{2}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
A numeric value stream measured over time, such as close price, volume, demand, or latency.
\sphinxbeforeendvarwidth
\end{varwidth}%
\\
\sphinxbottomrule
\end{tabulary}
\sphinxtableafterendhook\par
\sphinxattableend\end{savenotes}

\sphinxAtStartPar
Time\sphinxhyphen{}series value transforms require numeric \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Series}} threads. Time\sphinxhyphen{}axis
methods require a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Timeline}} or \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{TimeIndex}} thread.

\sphinxAtStartPar
This split is deliberate. A price column and a timestamp column have different
semantics even though both can be represented internally as arrays.


\subsubsection{Creating time features}
\label{\detokenize{manual/part08_time_series:creating-time-features}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
When you construct a frame in C++, use \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{pluss::make\_timeline}}:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{DataFrame}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{df}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{date}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pluss}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{make\PYGZus{}timeline}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
\PYG{+w}{        }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{2024\PYGZhy{}01\PYGZhy{}01T00:00:00Z}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,}
\PYG{+w}{        }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{2024\PYGZhy{}01\PYGZhy{}01T12:00:00Z}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,}
\PYG{+w}{        }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{2024\PYGZhy{}01\PYGZhy{}02T00:00:00Z}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{p}{,}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{close}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pluss}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{make\PYGZus{}series}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}\PYG{l+m+mf}{100.0}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m+mf}{105.0}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{l+m+mf}{103.0}\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{p}{,}
\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
When you load from CSV, parse or cast time columns early:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{n}{pluss}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{loader}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{ReadCsvOptions}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{options}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{n}{options}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{parse\PYGZus{}dates}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{date}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{p}{;}

\PYG{k}{auto}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{df}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{DataFrame}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{load\PYGZus{}csv}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{prices.csv}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{options}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
If a column loaded as text or as a numeric \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{YYYYMMDD}} series, cast it:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{auto}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{with\PYGZus{}time}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{df}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{cast}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
\PYG{+w}{    }\PYG{n}{pluss}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{table}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{DataFrame}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{CastSpec}\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}
\PYG{+w}{        }\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{date}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{pluss}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{table}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{ThreadCastTarget}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{Timeline}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{p}{,}

\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{cast(..., ThreadCastTarget::Timeline)}}, which is useful for market\sphinxhyphen{}data files that store dates as

\subsubsection{Sorting is your responsibility}
\label{\detokenize{manual/part08_time_series:sorting-is-your-responsibility}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
Time\sphinxhyphen{}series calculations use row order unless the method explicitly resamples or
aligns by a time axis. PlussMic will not sort a frame for you before computing a
return, lag, rolling mean, or line plot.

\sphinxAtStartPar
For ordered calculations, sort first:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{auto}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{sorted}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{df}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{sort\PYGZus{}values}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}\PYG{n}{DataFrame}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{o}{:}\PYG{n}{ArrangeSpec}\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{date}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nb}{true}\PYG{p}{,}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n+nb}{true}\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{k}{auto}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{returns}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{sorted}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{features}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{\PYGZob{}}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{close}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{\PYGZcb{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{ts}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{returns}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
This matters in production. A return computed on unsorted prices is not a
slightly messy return; it is a different calculation.


\subsubsection{Thread time\sphinxhyphen{}series accessor}
\label{\detokenize{manual/part08_time_series:thread-time-series-accessor}}
\sphinxAtStartPar
\sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Thread::ts()}} creates a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{TimeSeriesAccessor}} for one numeric \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Series}} payload:

\begin{sphinxVerbatim}[commandchars=\\\{\}]
\PYG{k}{auto}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{close}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{df}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{features}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{l+s}{close}\PYG{l+s}{\PYGZdq{}}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\PYG{k}{auto}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{r}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{o}{=}\PYG{+w}{ }\PYG{n}{close}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{ts}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{.}\PYG{n}{returns}\PYG{p}{(}\PYG{l+m+mi}{1}\PYG{p}{)}\PYG{p}{;}
\end{sphinxVerbatim}

\sphinxAtStartPar
The source thread must be defined, must be \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ThreadKind::Series}}, and must be
numeric. If you call \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{ts()}} on a \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Note}}, \sphinxcode{\sphinxupquote{Timeline}}, or non\sphinxhyphen{}numeric payload, the
operation throws when you call the accessor method.
